newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea a potential market for US grain - expert.
newsitem.headline: N. Korea a potential market for US grain - expert.

text.p: North Korea has the potential in the long term to become a growing commerical market for U.S. grain, but it will first have to address urgent credit problems and other infrustructure challenges, said an Agriculture Department expert on Asian markets.
"I think there's great potential there, but that's looking years down the road," said John Dyck of USDA's Economic Research Service.
North Korea will probably concentrate on imports of corn, wheat and rice, said Dyck, with corn imports dominating because of the low price.

Dyck said in an interview with Reuters Tuesday that North Korea needs to import a million tonnes or more of grain just for direct human food use, and could use at least another million tonnes of grain to develop its livestock production.

Long term, with its population of more than 22 million, North Korea's imports have the potential to be half as much as those of South Korea which buys about nine million to 10 million tonnes of corn a year, Dyck said. But he noted that that scenario "is not right around the corner" and depends largely on a drastic improvement in the country's economy.

North Korea is struggling with a terrible food shortage brought on by two consecutive years of crop-devastating floods. The United States announced Tuesday that it would be giving $15 million in additional food aid to the country. The State Department said the aid would be in the form of 50,000 tonnes of corn.

Dyck agreed with an assessment made earlier this month by Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman that in the near future, North Korea will be a greater recipient of U.S. food aid, than a commerical buyer of U.S. agricultural products.
"Looking three to four years down, they'll probably be mainly an aid recipient ... If you're talking about a fully commercial market, that's several years down the road," said Dyck.
Dyck said he would expect to see more small commercial purchases by North Korea similar to the barter deal recently worked out with Cargill Inc where 20,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat was swapped for zinc.

North Korea's ability to pay off some of its international debt and improve its credit rating, increase its fuel resources and expand its exports will be key to the country becoming a regular cash customer of the United States, Dyck said.

North Korea currently owes about a billion dollars to international lenders, mostly Japanese banks and institutions. "They have a very serious problem -- they can't get credit from anyone," said Dyck. "Taking a systematic approach to restore credit-ability is important."

Dyck said North Korea has been a fairly regular food importer in the past, and as recently as 1993, it imported 1.3 million tonnes of corn, wheat and rice. Lack of credit and money has forced the country to depend on its domestic agricultural production in recent years, and the USDA analyst said it has been a "heroic" effort that the country's system was able to sustain it as long as it did.
